title: Praying while traveling
hook: travelers shorten four-unit prayers to two, and may combine some

segments.voice: Yesterday, the khutbah, and your line: silence for the khutbah. Did someone get your whole hearing, with the phone in your pocket? Today we leave the mosque and hit the road. Day one thousand eighty-seven.

A highway rest stop, the engine ticking as it cools. A family has been on the road since breakfast, and the noon prayer has come in. The kids stretch their legs by a picnic table. Their father spreads a thin mat on the grass beside the car, faces the direction his phone gives him, prays, and is done sooner than he would be at home. Shorter than usual, and by design. Islam has a rule for the road, and it starts with a verse and a question someone once put to Umar. Today's word is the shortening.
screen: `A REST STOP, ENGINE COOLING.` → `A MAT ON THE GRASS.` → `SHORTER, BY DESIGN.`

segments.voice: Qasr means shortening. On a journey, the prayers of four units, the noon, afternoon and night prayers, are prayed as two. The dawn and sunset prayers stay as they are. First, the verse. Pickthall's translation of surah four says that when ye go forth in the land, "it is no sin for you to curtail (your) worship," and then adds a condition: if you fear an attack. Second, the question. A man named Ya'la asked Umar ibn al-Khattab about that condition. People are safe now, he said. Why do we still shorten? Umar said he had wondered the very same thing, and had asked the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, who answered: it is a charity God has given you, so accept His charity. That's in Sahih Muslim. Notice the word. Four days ago, two units of duha were a charity paid for your joints. Here the charity runs the other way. God gives it, and the traveler's job is to take it. Third, an old memory. Aisha said, in Sahih al-Bukhari, that the prayer was first prescribed as two units, and then the traveler's prayer was kept that way while the prayer at home was lengthened. On that report, the shortened prayer is the older shape, not a cut-down one. Fourth, combining. On journeys the Prophet sometimes joined the noon and afternoon prayers, or the sunset and night prayers, praying them one after the other. Here the schools part ways. The Hanafi school holds that shortening is required for a traveler, and allows combining only during the hajj, at Arafah and Muzdalifah. Other schools treat shortening as a permission and allow combining on journeys. They also differ on how far counts as a journey, and how long a stay ends it. Each school reads the same reports with care.
screen: `FOUR BECOME TWO.` · `NO SIN TO CURTAIL.` · `A CHARITY: ACCEPT IT.` · `THE SCHOOLS PART WAYS.` · then, large: `ACCEPT HIS CHARITY.`

segments.voice: The practice is to learn your school's rule. For now, settle, and notice what you're carrying in your body: shoulders up, a tight jaw, a hand gripping something. Let one thing go with each breath. Then bring to mind your next trip, near or far. If you pray, you can find out this week, from a teacher or a trusted book of your school, how far counts as a journey and whether you may combine. If you don't, notice one load you could set down on your next trip. The bell holds the time.
Qasr. Shortening: on a journey, the four-unit prayers are prayed as two, a charity from God to accept. Today's word.
Your line: lighter on the road. Today, when something offered makes a load lighter, take it without arguing, and say thanks. Day one thousand eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslims on a journey pray the noon, afternoon and night prayers as two units each, and depending on their school may combine noon with afternoon and sunset with night; schools set their own rules on distance and length of stay.

trapdoor: what you thought: travelers get to skip prayers.
what it means: the four-unit prayers are shortened to two, not skipped. dawn and sunset stay whole.
what a scholar hears: Aisha's report that prayer was first two units, so on that reading the traveler keeps the older shape.

notes: Editor: new hook (a highway rest stop) because the airport-gate, delayed-flight scene repeated day 1073's hook; 'two days ago' corrected to 'four days ago' for duha (day 1083); dropped 'brave enough' as an unsupported characterization of the questioner. The 'Gate twelve' note no longer applies.
Pickthall 4:101 quoted from memory ('And when ye go forth in the land, it is no sin for you to curtail (your) worship if ye fear that those who disbelieve may attack you'); confirm wording.

Muslim 686 (Ya'la ibn Umayyah, Umar, 'a charity ... accept His charity') paraphrased; Bukhari 350 (Aisha: prayer first enjoined as two rak'ahs) paraphrased; Bukhari 1107 cited for combining on journeys; confirm numbers.

Fiqh summary: Hanafi: qasr obligatory ('azimah) and jam' only at Arafah and Muzdalifah; Shafi'i, Hanbali, Maliki: qasr a concession or stressed sunnah, combining permitted for travel (with differences). Simplified; confirm. Distance and duration thresholds intentionally given without numbers.
'Gate twelve' is a scene detail, not a claim.
